name: graceful-degradation
intent: Keep the useful part of the system working when a dependency, subsystem or resource fails, hangs or saturates: detect the failure, deliberately drop or cheapen the non-essential work, and serve the parts that still work - with the degraded result marked as such.
problem: A dependency or subsystem fails, hangs or saturates, and the code treats the outcome as all-or-nothing: the whole request, page or service fails even though most of the work it performs never needed that dependency. The recurring decision is which functionality is essential, what a cheaper substitute looks like, and how the system switches between full and degraded behaviour without a deploy.
context: Long-running services and clients that compose several dependencies, caches or optional features - search and feeds, personalisation modules, checkout side effects, dashboards, media delivery - where availability and business continuity matter more than completeness, where a criticality ranking of functions exists or can be established, and where overload or dependency latency, not only bugs, is the expected trigger.
benefits: Availability stops being all-or-nothing: one failed dependency no longer fails the request, and the features that never needed it keep working.
Protects the surviving capacity: a degraded request does less work, so the resources left after a failure are spent on the functions that matter most.
Forces an explicit criticality ranking - which functions are essential and which may be dropped - which is information incident response needs anyway.
Cheaper than failover or a hot standby: a cached snapshot, a subset of results or a placeholder is available even when the dependency is not, and the switch is automatic.
User-visible continuity: a partial page with a notice is almost always better than an error page, and the same mechanism covers dependency failure and self-inflicted overload.
tradeoffs: The degraded path is a second implementation that is almost never exercised, so it rots; the SRE book's rule that the code path you never use is the code path that does not work applies literally, and testing or periodically triggering it is real effort.

Silent quality loss: stale, partial or approximated answers can look exactly like complete ones, and consumers act on them; without an explicit marker (flag, header, per-item status) the degradation is undetectable.
Permanent degradation: once a cheap fallback exists, the dependency stops being fixed, and the mode machine hides an error rate that should have been an incident.

Thresholds and mode machines bring their own failure modes: wrong thresholds never trigger or flap, and a complex policy can trip into degraded mode when it was not wanted or create feedback cycles between services.

Security and compliance can be weakened by accident - fallbacks that serve cached data without re-checking authorization, skip validation, or drop integrity checks are a classic way a degraded path becomes a vulnerability.
Debugging gets harder: a request can now succeed in several qualities, so responses, metrics and traces must carry the mode or operators cannot tell normal from degraded.

Cascading degradation: one degraded dependency can trigger degradation in a downstream service that depends on it, creating a cascade of correlated failures that a centralized degradation signal should prevent.
Stale-data compliance: serving cached responses in regulated domains (financial, healthcare, GDPR-sensitive) without re-checking authorization or freshness can violate compliance requirements.

participants.responsibility: The caller or user-facing layer that receives a partial or cheaper answer; the contract must let it tell a degraded result from a complete one so it does not treat a substitute as truth.
The full-fidelity realization of the function - live query, fresh computation, exact ranking - used while the dependency is healthy.
The cheaper substitute served while the primary path is unavailable: cached snapshot, subset of results, approximate algorithm, read-only mode or placeholder answer.
The signal that establishes a dependency is failing or saturated: error rate, circuit-breaker state, health check, latency or queue-length metric, capacity signal.
Maps detector state plus request criticality to a mode (full, degraded, shed), applies it consistently at one choke point, and owns the automatic switch back to full behaviour.

use_cases: Search or feed: while the ranking or index service is slow, serve cached or subset results with cheaper ranking instead of an error page.
Product page composition: drop recommendations, reviews or inventory widgets whose dependency failed while the product data itself still renders.
Checkout and payment: keep the purchase path working and defer or drop non-essential side effects (loyalty points, analytics, confirmation e-mail) when their services are down.
Read-only mode: a write path or primary database failure downgrades to serving cached, read-only content and queues or explicitly rejects writes.
Media delivery: fall back to a lower bitrate, resolution or an audio-only stream when bandwidth or a CDN edge degrades (adaptive degradation).
Model-backed features: when an inference service is saturated, serve an older or cheaper model, a shorter generation or a canned answer instead of failing the request.
CDN edge: serve stale-while-revalidate cached content when the origin is unreachable, or use Cloudflare Always Online to serve archived snapshots of static pages.
GraphQL: return partial data with null placeholders for failed field resolvers rather than failing the entire query, using nullable fields and error lists.
Database read replicas: when the primary is unavailable, serve reads from a replica with a known staleness bound; flag responses with a freshness timestamp.
Third-party API integration: when a rate-limited or slow third-party API fails, return cached results or a curated default rather than surfacing a 429 or timeout to users.

LLM model serving: build a fallback ladder (primary model → cached embeddings → smaller local model → rule-based heuristics → static safe default) so the system always returns an answer rather than failing a user request.

Netflix Hystrix: wrap a remote call in HystrixCommand and return getFallback() when execution times out, is rejected or the circuit is open; keep any networked fallback isolated in its own command and thread pool.

GraphQL execution: nullable field resolvers can return partial data alongside an errors array when one field fails, preserving independent fields while clients distinguish null or missing data from a complete response.

Cloudflare Always Online: when an origin is unreachable, serve a marked stale cached or Internet Archive snapshot of eligible static pages, while accepting that dynamic and uncached content still fails.
avoid_when: A batch job or CLI with a single dependent call: fail fast with a non-zero exit; a fallback would only hide the error.
When the dropped work must stay correct for consistency or compliance (ledger entries, audit records, regulated data): use a transaction, outbox or queue instead of serving a substituted result.
When the consumer cannot distinguish degraded from complete output: fix the contract first (marker, per-item status), otherwise callers silently act on degraded data.
When the cheaper path is simply the better product default: make it the default (reduced feature set, smaller model, TTL-bound cache) instead of maintaining a mode machine.
When the dependency is essential by definition (authentication, authorization, integrity checks): failing closed is correct - degrading there is a security hole, not resilience.
anti_patterns: Silent degradation: returning a cached or default value with no marker, metric or log, so callers and users treat an approximation as complete.
The permanent degraded mode: the fallback ships, nobody fixes the dependency, and the product quietly becomes the stub - including caches that never expire because the refresh keeps failing.
One global degraded flag: a single switch flips the whole system, coupling unrelated functions' availability and creating feedback cycles between services.
The untested fallback: the mode exists in code but is never executed, so it fails the first time it is needed (or leaks the resources it never had to clean up).

Degrading around security: the fallback serves cached responses without re-checking authorization, skips validation or integrity checks, or disables rate limiting - availability bought with a vulnerability.
Fallback loop: A degrades to B, B degrades to A, amplifying load and extending outage duration until the cycle is detected and broken.
Metric-confused degradation: degraded responses counted as success in availability metrics, giving operators a false sense of health while users receive silently degraded experience.
design_principles: Explicit criticality ranking first: degradation follows a stated order of essential, optional and droppable functions, not the order in which code was written.
Separation of policy from mechanism: what is allowed to be dropped and how the substitute is produced and marked are separate decisions.
Partial failure is normal, not exceptional: design the steady state so any single dependency can be absent, never compose all-or-nothing.
Fail closed where correctness or security is at stake; degrade only functions whose cheaper version is still safe and honest.
Observability is part of the degraded contract: every degraded answer must be countable and attributable (metric, header, per-item status).

Monotonic degradation ladder: define an explicit ordered hierarchy of degradation levels (e.g. healthy → cached → limited → read-only → static → error) so the system moves through them in order rather than skipping to total failure.
Degrade at the boundary, not deep inside the call graph: one choke point (gateway, facade, policy object) keeps the degradation policy auditable and prevents scattering.

Test the fallback path like the primary path: periodic chaos engineering or scheduled drills are the only reliable way to verify the degraded path works, because the code path you never use is the code path that breaks.
best_practices: Write down the criticality ladder and the accepted substitutes before implementing, and keep the list small enough to be reviewed.
Trigger degradation from a detector with hysteresis (breaker state, saturation threshold) and log the transitions, instead of ad-hoc try/catch spread over every call site.

Mark degraded responses explicitly (a degraded flag, a Warning/X-Degraded header, per-item status, or a structured error with degraded reason) so consumers and dashboards can tell the qualities apart.
Exercise the degraded mode on purpose - periodic chaos/load drilling or a scheduled trigger - because the rarely used path is the one that breaks.
Bound the substitute: TTL/max-age on cached fallbacks, no fabricated data, and a documented way to force degradation off when it misbehaves.
Alert on time spent in degraded mode: if the mode is on often, it is an incident and not normal operation.
Keep degradation at one choke point (gateway, facade or policy object) while the number of dependencies is small; per-call fallbacks scatter the policy until it is unauditable.
Design a fallback hierarchy per dependency: fresh data → cached data → simplified data → static default → error. Each level must have independent failure modes and not share fate with the primary.

Distinguish graceful degradation from graceful shutdown: shutdown is about releasing resources cleanly on termination; degradation is about maintaining function under partial failure during normal operation.
Pair hedged requests (duplicate calls to reduce tail latency) with circuit breakers; without a breaker, hedging amplifies load to a failing backend and turns a brownout into an outage.

Use feature flags as ops kill switches: a manually-controlled circuit breaker that turns off a non-essential feature without a redeploy. Test all toggles in both on and off states plus production config.

Validate degradation schemas end-to-end: when a fallback path activates, the consumer must handle the degraded response schema correctly. A common failure is the UI breaking on a field that is present in the primary response but absent in the degraded one.

Run game days: schedule failure injection exercises (recommendation dependency down, cache cluster degraded, database primary unavailable) and verify the fallback activates, the user experience is acceptable, and the system recovers cleanly.
Track degraded response rate as a first-class metric alongside success rate and latency. A rising degradation rate is an early warning sign of cascading failure.
